items.stem: A compliance team requires that every AI-flagged transaction above a risk threshold pass through a two-person sequential review, the second reviewer blind to the first, under a documented regulatory audit expectation. How should the architect handle this review workflow?

opts.t: Continue eliciting the cost of a missed versus falsely flagged transaction, since that determines the review workflow design.
Implement the two-person sequential blind review exactly as specified; it is the compliance-driven attestation requirement, not an implementation suggestion to optimize.
Propose a confidence-weighted single-reviewer model that the architect judges more efficient, then present it as an improvement to the sponsor.
Escalate to the sponsor's leadership that the two-step sequential requirement is unnecessarily slow and should be reconsidered before build starts.

items.whyRight: The two-person sequential blind review is tied to a documented regulatory audit expectation — an external attestation requirement, not a design preference the architect can trade away. However sound the engineering, a redesign that removes or reshapes that mechanism is out of scope; the architect implements it exactly as specified.

whyWrong.A: The workflow is already fixed by a named regulatory audit expectation; treating it as still open to a cost-of-error elicitation misreads an external attestation requirement as an unbounded design question.
whyWrong.C: Replacing the mandated two-person blind review with a more efficient single-reviewer design substitutes the architect's engineering preference for a constraint that is external and not tradeable against efficiency gains.
whyWrong.D: The two-person sequential review is the attestation the regulator requires, not a build-schedule inconvenience; framing it as negotiable misreads an external, non-negotiable constraint as an internal scheduling preference.

items.t1Clause: under a documented regulatory audit expectation

items.stem: A team's structured correction loop captures input, output, expected output, and reviewer for every fix in a document-extraction pipeline. A sponsor cites one thoroughly documented correction as proof the underlying issue is now fixed and won't recur. What should the architect do?

opts.t: Accept the documented correction as proof the issue is resolved, since the structured loop confirms it was captured correctly.
Check the accumulated evaluation set for whether this failure mode recurs across cases before crediting the fix.
Establish a new recurring review reporting real production performance against the agreed acceptance criteria.
Tell the sponsor no correction can be credited without a controlled experiment isolating the cause.

items.whyRight: The structured loop is correctly capturing input, output, expected output, and reviewer for each correction; that record is what determines whether a failure recurs. One documented correction, however thorough, is a single case — check the accumulated evaluation set for a recurrence pattern before crediting the fix.

whyWrong.A: A well-captured single case confirms the loop is working, not that the failure won't recur; recurrence is read from the accumulated record, not one entry.
whyWrong.C: The structured loop already exists and is functioning; the gap is reading one entry as proof, not a missing recurring mechanism to build.
whyWrong.D: The existing structured record can already settle recurrence without a new experiment; refusing to read it abandons evidence the loop already provides.

items.stem: A chunking-strategy choice made to fit a small context-window limit a year ago is now moot after a context-window upgrade. The only surviving design record is a slide summarizing the final approach. What should the architect have recorded to make that original decision reopenable?

opts.t: Record the decision, the rejected alternatives with their numbers, the trade-off accepted, and the context-window limit that drove the choice.
Check the recorded constraint and re-evaluate the decision now that the ceiling has changed.
Produce a comprehensive written description of the current architecture with detailed component diagrams for the receiving team.
Hold another recorded walkthrough covering the new context-window limit and how it affects the design.

items.whyRight: A decision record needs the decision, the rejected alternatives with their numbers, the trade-off accepted, and the constraint that drove the choice; only that lets the team check the ceiling change against the original reasoning and reopen the decision on evidence.

whyWrong.B: No constraint was ever recorded here, only a slide was kept, so there is nothing written to check against the new context-window limit.
whyWrong.C: A thorough description of the current design, however detailed, carries no reasoning; it cannot show whether the relaxed ceiling changes the original trade-off.
whyWrong.D: A second walkthrough transfers understanding once more to whoever attends, but leaves no written record the next reviewer can check against a future change.

items.t1Clause: the only surviving design record is a slide summarizing the final approach

items.stem: An automated invoice-triage tool ran cleanly across a 3-branch trial, misrouting one invoice in every 350 twice during the trial while staff caught and hand-corrected 15% of routed invoices. Leadership wants it rolled out to all 45 branches. Select two actions to take first.

opts.t: Treat the observed failure rate and review proportion as fixed percentages that hold unchanged at higher volume.
Plan for the 1-in-350 failure as a routine event at the new volume, not as a rare edge case.
Convert the 15% review proportion observed in the pilot into a staffing line sized to the projected rollout volume.
Size infrastructure capacity and rate limits for the new volume, and treat that as the binding constraint on readiness.

items.whyRight: A failure recurring twice during a 3-branch trial is frequent at fifteen times the volume across 45 branches, so it must be planned as routine, not rare. The 15% review load actually measured in the trial is the only sound basis for staffing the wider rollout.

whyWrong.A: The observed rates are exactly what must be re-examined at the new scale, not treated as fixed; freezing them skips the assumption audit that scaling requires.
whyWrong.D: Infrastructure and rate-limit sizing is real and necessary, but it is not the binding constraint here; the failure rate and review load are what actually bite at this scale.
